primaryKeyword: how to track whatsapp and phone leads in ga4
secondaryKeywords: measuring offline enquiries from organic search
h1: How to track WhatsApp and phone leads from organic search
metaTitle: Track WhatsApp and Phone Leads in GA4
metaDescription: In India most enquiries arrive by call or WhatsApp, where GA4 sees nothing. The cheap instrumentation that works, and what a click can never prove.
answer: GA4 can see the tap, never the conversation. Fire an event on your `tel:` and `wa.me` clicks, publish one phone number that appears nowhere else, carry the page reference inside the WhatsApp pre-filled message, and ask every enquirer one question at intake. That combination costs an afternoon and closes most of the gap.
takeaways: **A tap is not a conversation.** A `tel:` click event says someone opened the dialler. Whether they called, connected or bought is not in GA4 and will never be.
The cheap stack is three parts: **one website-only phone number**, **a WhatsApp link carrying the page reference**, and **one question asked at intake**. No platform required.
GA4's enhanced measurement already catches `wa.me` clicks as outbound clicks. `tel:` links are not outbound clicks and need a tag of their own — that omission is the single most common gap we find.
Call-tracking software starts earning its bill somewhere north of ~150 phone enquiries a month. Below that a second SIM does the same job.
If anyone's reporting — or guarantee — is denominated in leads, this instrumentation is the measuring instrument. Build it before the baseline, not after.

sections.h2: Why standard GA4 advice does not survive contact with Indian demand
body: Almost every GA4 tutorial assumes a funnel that ends inside a browser: a form, a thank-you page, a purchase event with a transaction ID. A large share of Indian enquiry demand does not end there. It ends in a call placed from a showroom car park, or a WhatsApp message at 10pm asking whether you deliver to Nashik.

Both of those leave your website before anything is measurable. The tap fires, the browser hands the visitor to the dialler or to WhatsApp, and your page unloads. Everything that decides whether it was a lead happens on a channel GA4 has no view into.

The result is an argument nobody can win. Organic sessions look flat, the phone rings more than it did in March, and neither side can prove a thing — because the only number that moved is the one nobody agreed to measure. That failure has a companion in reverse, which we covered in [organic traffic up but leads flat](/answers/organic-traffic-up-but-leads-flat).
bullets: Someone reading the number off your header and dialling it manually. No click, no event, no trace at all.
A chat started from your Google Business Profile rather than your site — a different surface entirely.
A tap inside an in-app browser, where the page can unload before the event reaches Google's servers.
A missed call at 7pm that your team returns on Monday and closes on Wednesday.
A number screenshotted and forwarded to the actual decision-maker, who calls you a week later.

callout.title: The under-reporting is directional, not random
callout.body: Every gap above hides the same kind of enquiry: high-intent, offline, and usually the most valuable. So GA4's picture is not merely incomplete, it is skewed against exactly the channel you are trying to justify. An agency that reports GA4 conversions without saying this out loud is either careless or counting on it.

sections.h2: The cheap stack, in three parts
body: You can spend a month building this properly. You can also get most of the answer by Friday. Start with the version that costs almost nothing, because it works whether or not the visitor tapped anything.

Alongside these three, fire the click events themselves. GA4's enhanced measurement already collects [an outbound click event whenever a visitor clicks a link that leads away from your domain](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9216061), which catches `wa.me` links with no tagging work at all. A `tel:` link is not an outbound click, so it needs a small tag of its own. Mark both as key events so they show up where you actually look.
numbered: **Publish one phone number that appears nowhere else.** Not your main line. A second number — a spare SIM in the same handset is fine — used only on the website. Every call to it came from the site. That is not attribution down to the query, but it is a clean channel split for about the cost of a basic prepaid plan, and no JavaScript can break it.

**Carry the page reference inside the WhatsApp pre-filled message.** A click-to-chat link accepts a pre-filled message. Encode the page and the source in it — something like `Hi, enquiring about the Kolhapur project (web / organic / pricing page)` — and your salesperson reads the origin in the chat itself, before they reply. GA4 loses the handoff; the message does not. Put [UTM parameters](/glossary/utm-parameters) on the link too, but treat the message text as the copy that survives.

**Ask one question at intake.** "How did you find us?", typed into your CRM by whoever picks up, every time, no exceptions. It is self-reported, it is imprecise, and it is still the most useful field you will add this quarter — because it is the only instrument that spans the channels analytics cannot see.

**Reconcile monthly, in one sheet.** CRM enquiries down one side, GA4 events down the other, matched on date. You are not looking for agreement. You are looking for the ratio between them, and for the month it changes.

sections.h2: What a tel: tap proves, and what it does not
body: This is the part most reports quietly skip. A click event on a `tel:` link means the visitor's phone opened its dialler with your number in it. It does not mean a call was placed. It does not mean anyone answered. It certainly does not mean a lead.

The gap between taps and conversations is real and it is not a fixed ratio. It moves with how busy your line is, what time of day your traffic peaks, and whether the tap was accidental — and on mobile, a surprising share of them are. Without call records you cannot know your own ratio, which is precisely why the second phone number earns its keep: it gives you the denominator.

So label the metric honestly. In every report we send, the event is called dialler opens, not calls. It sits with impressions and clicks as a leading indicator — useful, early, and not something anyone should be paid against. What gets counted as a lead is defined separately, and deliberately, in [what counts as a qualified lead from SEO](/answers/what-counts-as-a-qualified-lead-from-seo).

callout.title: The same logic applies to WhatsApp
callout.body: A wa.me click opens a chat window with your number loaded. Plenty of people never send the message. Unless you run the WhatsApp Business API and can read delivery and reply data, attribution ends at the click — and any agency claiming to track the conversation itself is guessing at best.

sections.h2: When call-tracking software is worth the bill
body: Call-tracking platforms swap the number shown to each visitor and stitch the resulting call back to a session, which gives you landing page, source and often a recording. It is genuinely good technology. It is also a recurring bill, an extra script on every page, and one more thing to break during a migration.
Our rule is volume, not sophistication. Below the threshold, the same information is available for the price of a SIM and five minutes of discipline at intake.

bullets: **Watch your Google Business Profile number.** Swapping the number in your listing for a tracking number risks a mismatch with your citations. Keep the listing on the real number and track the website separately.
**Recordings are a compliance question, not just a feature.** If you record calls, say so on the call and know where the recordings sit. That is a decision for your counsel, not your agency.
**Do not buy it to settle an internal argument.** If the disagreement is about whether SEO works, the fix is an agreed definition of a lead, not a subscription.

sections.h2: Wiring it into the baseline, so the number is settleable
body: Here is why we publish this rather than keeping it as an internal checklist. Our guarantee is written against your own numbers: we freeze your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search on day one, and if we have not beaten that figure in 90 days we keep working free until we do. See [how that works](/seo).

A baseline that counts only web-form submissions, on a business where four in five enquiries arrive by phone or WhatsApp, is not a baseline. It measures a sliver of the business and it moves for reasons nobody controls — a form redesign, a WhatsApp button added to the header, a seasonal shift in how people prefer to make contact.

So the instrumentation goes in first, in week one, before the baseline is frozen. Distinct number live, click events firing, intake question mandatory in the CRM, and 90 days of history reconstructed from whatever record already exists — call logs, the WhatsApp Business inbox, the receptionist's diary. Imperfect history is fine, as long as it is imperfect in the same way before and after.

Then the arithmetic is straightforward: leads counted the same way, measured over the same length of window, compared against a frozen number. Attribution beyond that point — which page, which query, which rupee — is a separate and harder problem, and we take it apart in [how to attribute revenue to SEO](/answers/how-to-attribute-revenue-to-seo).

callout.title: The one-line test
callout.body: Ask your agency: if a customer finds you on Google, calls the number in your header and buys, does that appear anywhere in the report you receive? If the answer needs more than one sentence, it does not.

sections.h2: Four ways this setup breaks quietly
body: None of these announce themselves. All four have cost clients we later picked up an entire quarter of measurement.
bullets: **A theme update replaces the header phone number** with a hard-coded one from the template demo. Calls keep arriving on a number nobody is watching. Check the rendered HTML after every deployment, not the page builder.

**Someone adds the tracking number to your Google Business Profile, IndiaMART listing and Justdial page** "for consistency". Now every channel reports as website. Consistency is right for your real number and wrong for your tracking one.
**The WhatsApp link gets rebuilt without the pre-filled message** because a developer tidied it. The clicks still fire; the origin is gone. It is the least visible regression on this list.

**The intake question stops being asked** three weeks in, because it feels rude when the caller is in a hurry. It is not rude, and it is the only field that survives a tooling change. Make it a required field, not a habit.

**Nobody reconciles.** GA4 says 40 dialler opens, the CRM says 12 enquiries, and both numbers get reported for a year without anyone asking why. The ratio is the finding. Look at it monthly, and get the underlying setup checked properly if it drifts — that is what our [analytics setup work](/services/analytics-setup-services) exists for.

faqs.a: No. GA4 can record the click that opens WhatsApp, and nothing after it. The conversation happens in an app Google Analytics has no access to. Everything beyond the click has to come from your WhatsApp inbox, your CRM, or the pre-filled message you encoded into the link.

faqs.q: How do I track click-to-call in GA4?
faqs.a: Fire an event on clicks to `tel:` links. Enhanced measurement will not do it for you — `tel:` links are not outbound clicks, so they need a tag of their own in Google Tag Manager or a small listener in your site code. Then mark the event as a key event and label it honestly as dialler opens.

faqs.q: Why does GA4 show fewer leads than my CRM?
faqs.a: Because most of your enquiries never touched a form. Calls placed from a manually dialled number, chats started from your Google Business Profile, and taps inside in-app browsers all land in the CRM and never reach GA4. A gap in that direction is normal. A gap that changes month to month is a broken tag.

faqs.q: Should I put UTM parameters on my WhatsApp link?
faqs.a: Put them on the link so the click is attributed in GA4, and put a readable page reference in the pre-filled message text so a human can see the origin in the chat. The parameters serve your analytics; the message serves your sales team. The second one is what actually gets used.

Below roughly 50 phone enquiries a month, no — a second phone number used only on the website answers the same question for the price of a prepaid plan. Above roughly 150 a month, dynamic number insertion starts paying for itself, because it tells you which landing page produced the call.

faqs.q: How do I count offline enquiries in an SEO baseline?
faqs.a: Instrument first, freeze second. Get the distinct number, the click events and the intake question live in week one, then reconstruct 90 days of history from call logs and the WhatsApp inbox. Imperfect history is acceptable as long as it is imperfect the same way on both sides of the comparison.
